subject: toyBox
pitch:
Category: Prop group.
Subject: open toy box spilling toys.
Style: your choice. Pick an unexpected, striking visual style that suits this subject (not the obvious one), name it in a comment at the top of the module, and commit to it everywhere.
reasoning:
I'm weighing distinctive visual styles for this toy module—considering constructivist propaganda aesthetics, Memphis-design 1980s boldness with squiggles and terrazzo patterns, or Scandinavian folk-art felt textures—before settling on a direction.

Memphis Group postmodern style feels right: terrazzo paint, zigzag trim, squiggle decals, flat saturated colors with thin black outlines, applied to a toy chest with spilled-out contents like blocks, a spinning top, a striped ball, a robot head, a teddy bear, a jack-in-the-box spring, marbles, jacks, a yo-yo, and dice. I'm planning the box dimensions and the open, tilted lid, aiming for a rich but manageable part count around 150-250, and since this is a static prop I don't need joints—just careful geometry construction using APIs I'm confident about.

Working through part construction and positioning: a box helper with rotation in degrees, floor-contact checks so everything's bottom sits at y=0, and overall height budgeting for the open lid plus spilled toys. Now I'm figuring out how to apply the terrazzo/Memphis confetti pattern to the box panels using a custom paint function with cell-based shapes.

I'm also planning additional decorative textures: a zigzag trim strip, a squiggle/confetti decal plane for the front panel, and a set of alphabet/number block textures (letter A, letter B, a numeral, and a star/dots pattern) to scatter as toy blocks.

For the remaining toys, I'm figuring out a striped beach ball using angle-based paint around a center point, a rubber duck with simple black eye spheres and an orange beak, and a tin robot built from a boxy head and body with antennae and SVG-based eye details.

Actually, a spring-loaded jester popping from the toy box sounds more fun—I could use a coil sweep from the clockwork kit for the spring and top it with a clown head.

For the face itself, decaling a texture onto a sphere seems risky since it wraps oddly; better to build the head from simple colored parts—sphere for the base, small shapes for eyes/nose/mouth, plus a cone hat with a pom—placing the face elements just slightly off the sphere's surface rather than trying to decal directly.

I should be fine assuming decals work without joints, as static models likely omit bone data entirely. Now I'm thinking through the box structure—building it as five open-top walls with a darker painted interior, then designing a hinged lid that rotates open from the back-top edge at a chosen angle.

Working out the rotation math for the lid's hinge: using a rotation about the X axis, I need to pick the sign of the angle so the lid swings forward and up correctly, verifying with the trig that the new z and y coordinates land where expected for an open lid position.

I'm settling on D=0.38 with a 100° opening angle, keeping total height around 0.75. For the lid faces, after rotating, the outer top surface points mostly backward and slightly down, while the inner surface faces the viewer -- so I'll decorate that inner face with a Memphis-style decal since it's now the visible side.

Working out the lid's local coordinate helper and rotating child decoration planes to match the lid's tilt using quaternion composition...

I'm defining a helper that computes lid part positions by rotating local coordinates around the hinge point using the lid's open quaternion, so each lid piece attaches correctly relative to the hinge axis.

Now I'm sketching out box dimensions: width 0.7, depth 0.45, height 0.38, with wall thickness 0.025, plus small feet raising the body off the ground. I'm also thinking about how the front wall should stay intact while toys appear to spill over the top edge rather than through an opening.

For the interior, I want a visibly different color from the exterior, so I'm planning thin liner panels inside the deep blue walls, with terrazzo-paint cladding on the outer faces, and considering Memphis-style striped accents on the corner posts.

I'm adding mustard-yellow striped corner rails, a pink striped top trim, and front panel decorations like a yellow disc, teal triangle, and textured zigzag planes positioned facing outward on each side, along with Memphis-style SVG confetti textures with transparent backgrounds.

For the lid interior, I'm sketching a bold "TOYS" lettering design using chunky sans-serif text with an offset shadow effect alongside decorative shapes, likely rendered as SVG text rather than hand-drawn paths.

I'm also planning additional block textures — letter blocks, a number block, and a star block each with colored rectangular backgrounds and borders — plus decal-style faces for a robot, a clown, and maybe a bear using simple eye/nose/mouth parts, and a dice texture with a repeating pip pattern applied uniformly across all cube faces.

Then I'm laying out the toy placement on the floor in front of the toy box: three alphabet blocks arranged with one stacked and one tilted on the box rim, each given tumbling rotations, followed by positioning a striped ball nearby.

Writing paint segmentation logic...

Now moving to the spinning top: a lathe shape tipped on its side near the box, defining a profile that flares out from a thin point into a rounded body.

Checking that the belly radius clears the floor with the tilt applied, then I'll move on to the rubber duck: building a sphere-based body and head, flat beak, eyes, wing, and tail cone, with a helper function to place and rotate each duck instance on the pile.

Writing pose and placement helper functions...

I'll use a shared low-poly unit sphere geometry for ball parts, generating a fresh instance each call to avoid mutation issues from the builder, and a unit box geometry scaled per dimension for block parts.

Now I'm thinking about placing the robot figure sitting inside the box, with its torso and head rising above the rim near the open lid, arms raised and body tilted forward-left using rotation offsets, while its legs stay hidden inside.

I'm designing the robot in a flat Memphis style with saturated colors—red torso with button details, yellow head using a textured face plane, plus antenna, side-mounted ear cylinders, rod arms with small claw-hand boxes raised up, and a small gear part on the chest for mechanical detail.

Next I'm sketching the teddy bear sitting at the front-right of the box: an ellipsoid body, spherical head with muzzle, nose, ears, eyes, arms, legs, and a patch, all in tan fur with a Memphis-style mottled paint treatment.

I decide to make it unexpectedly hot pink with a teal bow tie for a stylized Memphis look, positioned around (0.4, 0, 0.55), flopped with arms out. Then I plan a jack-in-the-box clown rising from the box on a leaning spring, with a sphere head, decal face, cone hat with pompom, and a torus ruff collar, checking that its height stays proportionate to the lid's top edge.

For the spring coil, I'm sweeping a thin tube along a helical path with a small radius and modest number of sides to keep the ring count reasonable. Now I'm adding a small wooden toy train engine near the front-left floor, with a boxy body, cab, cylindrical smokestack, four wheels, and a cowcatcher, styled in Memphis colors.

I'm also planning more scattered floor props: a handful of small glass marbles in a few colors, a textured die, a yo-yo made from a lathe shape plus a curved string sweep, and some flat confetti or paper-star cards laid on the floor.

I'll make a grey-white triangle texture with black outline and tint it per-call for variety, calling cards multiple times with different colors. I'll also add a spilled stacking-ring toy with a few tori lying scattered near the post for extra toy variety.

Tallying up the part budget across all the toys, I'm landing around 230 total pieces, which feels manageable.

Now I'm setting up a Memphis-style color palette with cream, pink, teal, yellow, blue, purple, red, black, orange, mint, and lilac tones, then working on terrazzo-style paint logic to scatter colored chips sparsely across a cream background.

Writing stripe and band helper logic...

Now I'm planning the box rim pieces along each edge with banded coloring, corner posts with diagonal stripe texture, hinge cylinders, and the lid structure with separate outer terrazzo skin and inner texture plane.

Adding support rods on each side of the lid for realism. For the lid's inner decoration, I'm designing a cream-colored texture with bold "TOYS!" text using a shadowed, blocky font styled via SVG.

Now I'm composing the front panel texture with a playful mix of shapes—a yellow circle, pink triangle, teal squiggle, zigzags, dots, and plus signs—arranged carefully within a wide rectangular viewBox to decorate the front of the toy box.

Now I'm designing a zigzag texture for a band under the rim, sizing planes with a 10:1 aspect ratio and placing them on front and side panels, reusing the same texture across multiple surfaces.

Setting the rim position at the top of the walls and placing the zigzag band and front panel art within the body height, with a colored base plinth strip near the bottom. Now I'm working out the box wall dimensions and positions, with blue interior walls and a thin terrazzo cladding skin on the outside faces.

Adding corner feet, a bottom board, and planning the open-top interior view: a pile of colored spheres and cubes scattered inside the box using randomized positions to look like toys peeking out.

I'm also adding some spilled toys around the box's base and rim — a tilted block, a duck perched on the edge, and maybe a slinky toppling over the side for a lived-in, scattered look.

For the slinky itself, I'm thinking of sweeping small torus rings along a curved arc path from the rim down to the floor, each ring oriented to follow the tangent of the path so it reads as a coiled spring cascading out.

I'm plotting the slinky's path spilling from the box over the front wall down to the floor, adjusting each torus ring's tilt and center height so the bottom edge just grazes the floor without clipping through it.

I'm sketching coordinates for the slinky's descending path and repositioning the stack ring toy, then starting to lay out where the train piece should go on the floor relative to everything else.

I continue placing pieces: the stacking ring toy toward one side, the bear nearby with a slight yaw, and two ducks positioned near the rim, with one duck resting partly on top of the rim edge.

Now I'm working out the blocks: a couple stacked at angles near the center-left, a star-shaped block rotated on the floor, and another block tilted as if resting against the rim. Finally I'm placing a small ball off to the side, sitting at floor level with a modest radius.

Scattering confetti cards across the box floor toward the camera, then positioning the robot and clown figures within the scene—robot leaning forward on the left with torso, head, face plane, ears, and antenna coordinates being defined, clown placed to the right.

Working out the robot's raised V-shaped arms with claw hands, plus chest details like a small gear and three button cylinders. I'm checking the vertical placement so the torso partially hides behind the front wall rim, giving a nice "emerging from the box" effect while keeping the robot and clown positions from overlapping in x.

For the clown, I'm sketching a spring neck coiling up from the torso to the head, using a sweep geometry for the coil, then placing a cream-peach sphere for the head with a decal for the clown face — diamond eyes, big smile, and a red nose that could be either a flat decal or a separate 3D sphere for more depth.

I'm adding a conical striped hat with a pom-pom on top, orange sphere tufts for hair on either side, and a scalloped ruff collar using a rotated torus geometry, all mounted above a small striped box body to complete the jack-in-the-box silhouette. Then I need to apply the clown decal onto the head sphere with proper positioning and facing direction.

For the bear, I'll build its face using plain geometric parts instead of decals—small black spheres for eyes and nose—and I'm now working out precise placement, scale, and color for its ellipsoid body, lighter belly patch, and head geometry at a sitting pose.

Still placing bear geometry...

Still placing duck geometry... tail, head, beak, eyes, wings, and cheek details, then thinking about adding a second duck on the rim, maybe in a different color for variety.

Now I'm shifting to designing a small train figure positioned and rotated to face into the scene, building out its chassis, boiler, smokestack, and cab with distinct colors for each part.

Still placing wheels, hub details, headlamp glow, cowcatcher, boiler stripe, and considering adding a small tender wagon behind it.

Now I'm designing a ring-stack toy: a blue base disc, a tapered yellow center post, and five stacked torus rings in descending sizes colored pink, teal, orange, purple, and red, oriented horizontally and spaced up the post.

I'm leaving the stack partially filled with only three rings on the post, a yellow sphere finial on top, and two rings scattered on the floor nearby, one lying flat and one leaning against a block.

For the yo-yo, I'm thinking of modeling it from two truncated cone halves plus a center axle rather than a full lathe profile.

Now I'm adding a thin black string curving along the floor from the yoyo's edge, then placing marbles with cycling colors at a fixed radius, and a textured die rotated slightly and resting on the floor beside everything.

For the alphabet/number blocks, I'm designing each face as a full-square SVG with a colored background, bold centered letter with black outline stroke, Memphis-style corner dots, and a star variant with purple background and yellow star shape -- mapping these onto a BoxGeometry so every face shows a drawn tile.

For tilted boxes resting on the floor or rim, I'm writing a helper that computes the correct resting height by rotating the box's eight corners through a quaternion and finding the lowest point, so leaning or tipped blocks sit flush against the surface instead of floating or clipping through it.

For scattered confetti, I'm placing flat triangle and squiggle cards on the floor using a cards helper with randomized spin, tinted colors, and slight mirroring for variety, planning a handful per color across a few shapes to keep the pile looking natural.

I catch that one of my near-grey hex colors actually registers as a tint due to channel variance, so I need to switch it to a purer grey like #222222 to keep that texture correctly colorless. I'm also checking for z-fighting on the flat floor cards and considering how to make glowing robot eyes work when they're baked into a face texture rather than being separate geometry.

Glow applied to a textured plane should preserve the dark parts of the texture while brightening the colored regions, which works well for the robot head's face. I'm deciding against adding glow to other elements like train headlamps, the ring toy, the clown's nose, or marbles, and I'm planning the imports needed from the glow and clockwork kits along with the meta export and a top-of-file style comment describing the Memphis Group aesthetic.

Writing imports and setup...

Writing part placement helper...

Defining geometry factory helpers...

Adding more geometry helpers...

Still writing beach ball coloring logic...

Now I'm defining the lid's hinge position and rotation, setting up constants for width, depth, and tilt angle so the lid rotates around a hinge point at the back edge.

Checking the math, I realize the open lid at -102° extends too high relative to the box height—around 0.87 versus the box's 0.38—so I need to shrink the lid's depth to keep proportions reasonable.

Setting D=0.40, W=0.66 brings the lid top to roughly 0.81, which still feels tall but acceptable for a toy box with chunky proportions; I could also reduce the tilt angle slightly or make the box itself taller instead. I'm verifying the lid doesn't clip into the floor when tilted back, and the hinge-to-top z distance checks out fine. Now I'm working out the inner face plane of the lid, located at local y=0 on the bottom of the lid body.

I'm sizing the plane to roughly match the drawing's aspect ratio and reasoning through the rotation so the texture orients correctly once the lid tilts open — making sure the drawing's top faces the right direction and that left/right isn't mirrored when viewed from the front.

Now I'm thinking about adding a thin inner frame strip around the lid's inner perimeter to distinguish it from the outer blue body.

For the lid itself, I'm layering a thin terrazzo skin box slightly offset outward, adding a small pink knob on the outer face as a grip, and connecting support straps as black rods between lid points.

Adjusting strap endpoint x-position so it aligns between lid and box width, then adding bolt caps at each end. I'm also laying out the painted rim pieces around the front, back, and sides, and starting on the interior wall blocks for the box.

Calculating outer skin panel positions...

Still placing geometry...

For sides I'll reuse the front texture at the appropriate plane size, positioning each face just outside the box walls. I'll skip decorating the back since it's hidden, but still give it a terrazzo skin to avoid showing raw color. Then I'm starting on the pile of interior contents using a seeded random generator to scatter items inside the box.

Now I'm placing those pile items with randomized x/z offsets and y heights so they peek slightly above the rim without worrying too much about overlap with other characters, alternating cube and sphere shapes with cycling colors, and then moving into defining the robot's pose and body parts.

Writing robot body parts...

Still computing claw positions...

Still building the robot parts...

Adding the clown face decal for painted features, then building the pointed hat with a brim and pompom on top, positioning each piece relative to the head.

Still positioning arms and hands...

Actually, I'll simplify the jack-in-box clown: skip arms entirely, put the head straight on a spring with a ruff collar, keeping the hat reaching near the lid top. Now I'm setting up a duck-shape helper function and planning a rainbow-colored slinky path using a smooth curve through points.

Writing slinky torus loop...

To flatten the curve near the end, I'll add an extra point at [-0.53,0.058,0.74] so the tangent goes horizontal there, keeping the ring bottom right at zero. Then I'm checking the train pose and starting to lay out marble positions on the scene.

Marbles: I'll scatter a cluster of twelve near the ring toy area (x in [0,0.5], z in [0.75,1.0]) plus four near the box, using a random generator rather than hardcoding every position. For confetti, I'm generating fourteen triangular card frames scattered across x[-0.75,0.75], z[0.25,1.0], configuring them with lean, mirror, and spin parameters so each card faces a random yaw, colored pink, with a small y offset above the floor.

Checking that `rng(seed)` returns a callable random number generator function, which matches how it's used as `rand` elsewhere in the kit for scattering effects.

Now I'm working out the lathe outline for a spinning top — mapping out the x,y points along its profile from tip to crown so the lathe operation can revolve it into a solid shape.

I'm planning the paint bands for the top's stripes using pink, teal, and yellow colors along its axis, and now I'm positioning the top itself relative to the bear, figuring out its tip location and axis direction so it sits correctly in the scene layout.

Checking the lathe axis of the top to make sure its lowest point stays just above the floor, I'm adjusting the tip height down to around 0.036 so it clears without overlapping. Now I'm starting to set up the pose for the first duck.

Repositioning duck1 to avoid overlap with the block stack, moving it to roughly (-0.05, 0.58). For the blocks, I'm sketching a stack of two tilted blocks plus a third block leaning at an angle resting on an edge near x=-0.13.

I'm placing the die, ring toy, and bear around the scene, then writing a `restBox` helper that computes the correct resting height for a rotated box by finding the lowest corner after rotation. I'm also defining how blocks get placed using position, quaternion, scale, and texture through a shared `put` function.

Now I'm positioning the rim block, the ball, and checking that the sphere's low pole sits exactly on the floor at y=0. I'm starting to sketch the train's pose details next.

Building the train chassis and boiler...

Still placing wheels and hubs...

Still placing wagon details...

Still building the stacking ring toy...

Writing bear construction code...

Still placing facial features and arms...

Adding toe pads, then a bow tie with a small teal ball and two cone-shaped wings angled outward from center.

Placing the duck at the rim top with a slight tilt, then thinking through the robot face texture: a dark rounded background, glowing cyan square eyes with pupils, a grille mouth with colored lines, and red cheek dots. Starting to write the SVG markup for this...

Designing the clown face now with pink cheeks, diamond-pupil eyes, and a big red smile against a transparent background.

Still writing die face and block SVG markup...

Designing the box lid layout with a cream rounded background, a dashed inner border, and a layered "TOYS" title with pink shadow and yellow fill outlined in black, surrounded by playful teal circles, purple triangles, and squiggles.

I'm adjusting the font size down to fit the text within the shapes without overlap, drawing it above the other elements, and considering small supporting text like "OPEN ME!" or "PLAY ALL DAY". Then I'm sizing the lid and front SVGs consistently at 640, and building a zigzag pattern strip with a yellow background and black polyline for the banding detail.

I simplify the zigzag to a single teal polyline with a thinner black stroke layered on top instead of overcomplicating it with pink polygons. I tally up the twelve textures needed (FRONT, ZIG, LID, BLK_A, BLK_B, BLK_1, BLK_STAR, ROBOT, CLOWN, DIE, TRI, SQUIG) and start thinking about how the glow effect depends on matching material names to the face texture.

Checking that the SDK accepts texture and scale array options in the part builder, and confirming the lighting setup and floor contact for all the toys sit correctly at y=0 given the overall height and width constraints. I decide to loosely type the extras parameter as `any` to avoid TypeScript signature conflicts when spreading options into the part builder.

Working out gear geometry parameters and slinky curve points as typed tuples, then starting to write a helper function that computes the resting height for an object based on its size and rotation by transforming its corners.

Now I'm planning block placement for a stack, calculating each block's y-position from the resting height plus offsets and figuring rotation angles so each piece leans naturally against the ones below it.

I'll keep the toy set simple with these few pieces, decide against adding extra elements like a kite or caterpillar, and settle on a color palette of roughly 16 defined hex values plus a few extras, staying under the material limit. Writing palette definitions...

Now I'm writing the paint function for the beach ball, setting up its center, orientation vectors, and a striped color pattern across six colors by checking distance along rotated axes.

Still writing paint pattern logic...

I notice the top shape slightly overlaps the duck, so I'll reposition the duck a bit further out to avoid the collision, then move on to defining the bear's ground pose and setting up the lathe call with its axis, segments, and color parameters.

For the pile of objects I'll randomize colors cyclically, and skip the confetti/ribbon idea as an extra feature for now. Writing the hinge cylinders for the lid, positioning them symmetrically on either side with rotation and scale so the lid pivots correctly at the box height...

Adjusting the hinge height so the closed lid doesn't clip through the rim, checking rim top versus hinge y-position to avoid overlap. Adding the lid body, skin, knob, inner plane, and pink edge trim strips at the lid's free end, sized to match the box width with a small border overhang.

Now I'm positioning the lid body and inner plane dimensions to properly cover the box's z-extent, then working out the strap and bolt placement on the box sides so the hinge mechanism aligns with the plinth and outer skin without floating or clipping.

I'm also locking in the final chest dimensions (W=0.66, D=0.40) and front panel art plane ratios, then starting to write the full build function.

Writing the build function...

Still writing duck geometry...

Adding the hat's pom-pom and finishing the ring-stack torus geometry with proper rotation and color, then double-checking that all variable names resolve cleanly before writing the final output.
